title.text: Measuring a model: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC and AUC, thresholds, baselines, overfitting

objects.text: How do I know whether a model is any good, and what should I ask the vendor who says it is?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 3 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome back. Session 2 ended on a warning: a single high score means little until you know how it was tested, and a deep tree can score perfectly on the cases it learned from and worse on new ones. Today we test the tests. A smoke alarm teaches every measure, one at a time, then you see them on a real result table, you move a threshold, and you meet a model that scores ninety percent by doing nothing.

slides.notes:
That question breaks into three things you can do by the end of today. You can read a confusion matrix and work out accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from it, with a pencil. You will spot three ways a model looks good without being good: accuracy with no baseline, one number that hides the threshold, and overfitting.

And you leave with a one-page question sheet that you can put to any vendor, about the numbers behind their claim. There are no tests today.

title.text:
Your two hours: a smoke alarm, then a real
result table, then your own pencil work

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_9b69cc17.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: The invoice numbers come from a run recorded in advance. Ask me to rerun it live.

slides.notes:
To get there, here is how the two hours run. The ideas take fifty minutes, because we build each measure slowly, one per slide, on a smoke alarm everyone knows: the four outcomes, accuracy, the baseline, precision, recall, F1, the threshold, the ROC curve and AUC. Then the same measures on a made-up late-payment model for Nile Valley Foods, with the cost of each mistake, and overfitting.

Two demonstrations take fifteen minutes. After the break you spend twenty minutes with a pencil on twenty real cases. We finish with your own work and the question sheet you can put to any vendor.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  How does a decision tree reach its answer?
2.  What is overfitting, and how did Session 2 test for it?
3.  How does a k-nearest neighbours model decide?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png
objects.alt: Three questions

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 2. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. How does a decision tree reach its answer? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. It asks a chain of yes or no questions about the features of the case, from the top down, until it reaches a leaf that gives the answer. The questions are learned from the training data.

Question two. What is overfitting, and how did Session 2 test for it? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. The model fits its training data, noise included, and does worse on new data. Session 2 tested on held-out data with k-fold cross-validation: train on k minus 1 folds, score the held-out fold, rotate, and average the fold scores.

Question three. How does a k-nearest neighbours model decide? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. It finds the k training examples most like the new one, using a distance, and gives the answer most of them had.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text:
How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_chain_11.90x4.45_0269f1f0.png
objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

objects.text: Each session is built on the ones before it.

slides.notes:
So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold training, validation and test data from Session 0 and a decision tree that can overfit from Session 2. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, ROC/AUC.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 4: turning words into numbers we can measure. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A table that counts the four kinds of outcome of a classifier: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.
Precision: of the cases flagged, the share that were real. Recall: of the real cases, the share that were flagged.
The score at or above which the model says positive. You choose it, and moving it trades false alarms for misses.
ROC: the true positive rate against the false positive rate, one point per threshold. AUC: the area under it, from 0.5 (coin flip) to 1.
A simple reference model to beat, such as the majority-class baseline that always predicts the most common class.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Confusion matrix. A table that counts the four kinds of outcome of a classifier: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

Precision and recall. Precision: of the cases flagged, the share that were real. Recall: of the real cases, the share that were flagged.

Threshold. The score at or above which the model says positive. You choose it, and moving it trades false alarms for misses.

ROC curve and AUC. ROC: the true positive rate against the false positive rate, one point per threshold. AUC: the area under it, from 0.5 (coin flip) to 1.

Baseline. A simple reference model to beat, such as the majority-class baseline that always predicts the most common class.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
A smoke alarm can be right in
two ways and wrong in two ways

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_stories_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A smoke alarm can be right in two ways and wrong in two ways

objects.text: Invented numbers: smoke or heat rose 1,000 times in a kitchen. 20 were real fires.

runs.text: Rang 50 times: 16 fires, 34 with no fire.
Silent 950 times: 4 fires, 946 with no fire.
Every event lands in exactly one box.

slides.notes:
Those five words all rest on one simple table, and I will build it from a story before I give it any names. Think of a smoke alarm in a busy kitchen. Over a year, smoke or heat rose one thousand times. Twenty times there was a real fire.

The other nine hundred and eighty were cooking, toast or a kettle. The alarm rang fifty times: sixteen real fires and thirty-four with no fire. It stayed silent nine hundred and fifty times: four times while a real fire burned, and nine hundred and forty-six times when all was well.

Check the sums with me: sixteen plus four is twenty fires, and all four boxes add to a thousand. These numbers are invented for the lesson. Which box worries you most?

title.text:
Name the four boxes and
you have a confusion matrix

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_named_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Name the four boxes and you have a confusion matrix

objects.text: Positive: the alarm says "fire", the thing we look for. True or false: was that answer right?

runs.text: TP: said fire, rightly.
FP: said fire, wrongly.
FN: said no fire, wrongly.
TN: said no fire, rightly.

slides.notes:
Most people worry about the four missed fires, and now each box gets its standard name. Two words do the work. Positive means the alarm said yes, fire, the thing we look for. Negative means it said no. True or false then says whether that answer was right.

So a true positive is a yes that was right: sixteen. A false positive is a yes that was wrong, a false alarm: thirty-four. A false negative is a no that was wrong, a missed fire: four. A true negative is a no that was right: nine hundred and forty-six.

The table is called a confusion matrix because it shows where the model confuses one answer with the other. Session 0 showed one for spam. From here on I use the short forms TP, FP, FN and TN.

title.text: Accuracy asks: how often was the alarm right?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_measure_7.70x4.80_78efb027.png
objects.alt: Accuracy asks: how often was the alarm right?

objects.text: Accuracy: the right answers divided by all the answers.

runs.text: The right answers are the gold boxes, TP and TN.
Range 0% to 100%. Higher looks better, with a catch.

slides.notes:
With the four counts named, the first and most obvious question is: how often was the alarm right?

The right answers are the two gold boxes, the true positives and the true negatives. Add them: sixteen plus nine hundred and forty-six is nine hundred and sixty-two. Divide by all one thousand events: zero point nine six two, which as a percentage is ninety-six point two. Now the general formula, in words: accuracy equals TP plus TN, divided by all four counts added together.

Accuracy runs from zero to one hundred percent, and higher looks better. Ninety-six point two sounds excellent. Before we celebrate, let me put it next to the simplest alarm you could possibly build.

title.text:
A baseline is the score to beat: an
alarm that never rings is 98% accurate

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_alarm_base2_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A baseline is the score to beat: an alarm that never rings is 98% accurate

objects.text: Baseline: a simple reference model. The majority-class baseline always gives the most common answer.

runs.text: Class: one of the answers a model chooses between.
No fire is the majority class: 980 of 1,000.
Accuracy 98%, yet it catches 0 of 20 fires.

slides.notes:
Here is that simplest alarm: it never rings at all. To judge any model we compare it with a simple reference like this, called a baseline. Each possible answer, fire or no fire, is called a class, and the class that occurs most often is the majority class.

Here no fire happened nine hundred and eighty times in a thousand. An alarm that always says no fire gets every one of those right: nine hundred and eighty divided by a thousand is ninety-eight percent accuracy. That beats our real alarm at ninety-six point two, yet it catches none of the twenty fires.

When the thing you look for is rare, accuracy rewards doing nothing. So we need measures that look straight at the fires. What is rare in your business?

title.text:
Precision asks: when the alarm
rings, how often is there a fire?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_measure_7.70x4.80_3124d829.png
objects.alt: Precision asks: when the alarm rings, how often is there a fire?

objects.text: Use only the top row: the times the alarm rang.

runs.text: Range 0% to 100%.
High precision: few false alarms, so people trust the ring.

slides.notes:
Accuracy mixed the fires with the quiet events, so the first focused measure looks only at the times the alarm rang, the top row. It rang sixteen plus thirty-four times, fifty in all. In sixteen of those there was a real fire. Sixteen divided by fifty is zero point three two, thirty-two percent.

That is precision. In general: precision equals TP divided by TP plus FP, the right yeses over all the yeses. It runs from zero to one hundred percent. High precision means few false alarms. Ours is low: two rings in three are toast. The never-ringing alarm has no precision at all, because it never rang and you cannot divide by zero.

Precision says nothing about the fires the alarm missed, so we need a second question.

title.text:
Recall asks: of the real fires,
how many did the alarm catch?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_measure_7.70x4.80_920b7aa3.png
objects.alt: Recall asks: of the real fires, how many did the alarm catch?

objects.text: Use only the left column: the real fires.

runs.text: Range 0% to 100%. High recall: few misses.
Also called the true positive rate (TPR) or sensitivity.
Never-ringing alarm: 0 ÷ 20 = 0%.

slides.notes:
The second question looks down the left column, the real fires. There were sixteen plus four, twenty fires. The alarm rang for sixteen of them. Sixteen divided by twenty is zero point eight, eighty percent. That is recall. The formula in words: recall equals TP divided by TP plus FN, the fires caught over all the fires.

High recall means few misses. The never-ringing alarm caught none of the twenty, so its recall is zero, and its ninety-eight percent accuracy is exposed at once. Recall is also called the true positive rate, TPR for short, or sensitivity. Keep the name TPR, because the ROC curve uses it.

Our alarm now has two numbers, thirty-two and eighty. Can we fold them into one?

title.text:
One number for precision and
recall: why a plain average misleads

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_avg_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: One number for precision and recall: why a plain average misleads

objects.text: A cautious alarm rang only twice, both times for a real fire. Invented numbers.

runs.text: Cautious: precision 2 ÷ 2 = 100%, recall 2 ÷ 20 = 10%.
Plain average 55%, almost the same as our 56%.
Yet it misses 18 of 20 fires.

slides.notes:
To compare two alarms it helps to have one number, and the obvious one is the plain average: add the two and divide by two. Watch it fail. Take a cautious alarm that rang only twice, both times for a real fire. Its precision is two over two, a hundred percent.

Its recall is two over twenty, ten percent. The average is a hundred plus ten, divided by two: fifty-five percent. Our alarm averages thirty-two plus eighty, divided by two: fifty-six percent. The two alarms look equal, yet the cautious one let eighteen of the twenty fires burn. A plain average lets one excellent number hide a terrible one.

We need an average that stays close to the weaker number, and the harmonic mean does exactly that.

title.text:
F1 score: the harmonic mean
stays close to the weaker number

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_f1steps_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: F1 score: the harmonic mean stays close to the weaker number

objects.text: Three steps: one over each number, average them, one over the result.

slides.notes:
The fix is called the harmonic mean, and it takes three steps. Step one: take one over each number. For the cautious alarm, one over one is one, and one over zero point one is ten. A small number turns into a big one, so the weak recall now dominates.

Step two: average them, one plus ten, divided by two, five point five. Step three: one over that, zero point one eight. So F1 is eighteen percent, close to the weak ten. For our alarm the same steps give forty-six percent. In one line, F1 equals two divided by one over P plus one over R, which tidies to two times P times R over P plus R, where P is precision and R is recall.

F1 runs from zero to one and reaches one only when both are perfect.

title.text:
The alarm reads a smoke score and
rings when it reaches the threshold

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_alarm_thr_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The alarm reads a smoke score and rings when it reaches the threshold

objects.text: Threshold: the score at or above which the model says positive. You choose it.

runs.text: Score: a smoke reading from 0 to 10.
Grey: scores at cooking and toast. Red: at real fires.
The two overlap, so no threshold is perfect.

slides.notes:
So far the alarm simply rang or stayed silent, but where does that answer come from?

An alarm measures smoke and gives a score, here from zero to ten. It rings when the score is at or above a set line. That line is the threshold, and someone chooses it. The grey hill shows the scores at ordinary events such as cooking and toast; most are low.

The red hill shows the scores at real fires; most are high. Where the hills overlap, some toast scores higher than some small fires, so wherever you put the line, something lands on the wrong side. Most machine learning classifiers work the same way: a score, then a threshold.

Let me show you the counts for the three lines in the picture.

title.text:
Move the threshold and the errors trade
places: fewer misses, more false alarms

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_alarm_table_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Move the threshold and the errors trade places: fewer misses, more false alarms

objects.text: Same 1,000 invented events. Lower threshold: recall rises, precision falls.

slides.notes:
Here are the three lines from the picture, on the same thousand events. With the high threshold the alarm rings twenty times: twelve fires caught, eight false alarms, eight fires missed. Precision is twelve over twenty, sixty percent, and recall twelve over twenty, also sixty. Our setting rings fifty times: precision thirty-two, recall eighty, as we worked out.

The low threshold rings two hundred times: nineteen fires caught, a hundred and eighty-one false alarms, one fire missed. Precision falls to nineteen over two hundred, nine and a half percent, while recall rises to ninety-five. Read down the table: lowering the threshold trades misses for false alarms, and no row is free.

Which row would you choose for a kitchen, and which for a hospital ward?

title.text:
False positive rate asks: of the events
with no fire, how often did it ring?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_measure_7.70x4.80_8f486d44.png
objects.alt: False positive rate asks: of the events with no fire, how often did it ring?

objects.text: Use only the right column: the events with no fire.

runs.text: Range 0% to 100%. Lower is better.
TPR looks at the fires. FPR looks at the non-fires.
Short form: FPR.

slides.notes:
To show every threshold in one picture we need one more rate, built like recall but on the other column. Look only at the events with no fire: thirty-four plus nine hundred and forty-six, nine hundred and eighty. The alarm rang during thirty-four of them. Thirty-four over nine hundred and eighty is zero point zero three five, three and a half percent.

That is the false positive rate, FPR for short: FP divided by FP plus TN, the false alarms over all the quiet events. Lower is better. Notice the pair. The true positive rate, recall, asks how many fires got a ring. The false positive rate asks how many quiet events got a ring. A good alarm has the first high and the second low.

title.text:
Plot each threshold as a point, join the
points, and you have the ROC curve

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_roc_build_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Plot each threshold as a point, join the points, and you have the ROC curve

objects.text: Along: false positive rate. Up: true positive rate. Dashed: ringing at random.

slides.notes:
Now we put the two rates together, one point per threshold. Each row of the table is one alarm setting: its false positive rate goes along the bottom, its true positive rate up the side. The high threshold gives zero point eight percent and sixty percent. Our setting gives three and a half and eighty.

The low threshold gives eighteen and ninety-five. Add the two extremes: an alarm that never rings sits at zero and zero, one that always rings at a hundred and a hundred. Join the points and you have the ROC curve, short for receiver operating characteristic, a name from early radar work.

The dashed diagonal is an alarm that rings at random, as likely for toast as for fire. A good curve hugs the top left corner.

title.text:
AUC, the area under the ROC curve, is the
chance that a fire outscores a quiet event

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_auc_pairs_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: AUC, the area under the ROC curve, is the chance that a fire outscores a quiet event

objects.text: AUC: area under the curve. 1 is perfect, 0.5 is a coin flip.

runs.text: Five events give 2 × 3 = 6 fire and no-fire pairs.
Below 0.5: worse than a coin flip.
AUC needs no threshold.

slides.notes:
The whole curve can be summed up in one number: the share of the square that lies under it, called AUC, the area under the curve. It has a plain meaning, which this small example shows. Take five events: two fires, with smoke scores eight and six, and three quiet events, scoring seven, three and two.

Pair every fire with every quiet event: two times three, six pairs. In five pairs the fire has the higher score. Only six against seven goes the wrong way. Five out of six is zero point eight three, and that is exactly the AUC for these five events.

So AUC is the chance that a randomly chosen fire scores above a randomly chosen quiet event. One is perfect, and zero point five is a coin flip. No threshold was needed.

title.text:
All five measures on one page,
with the smoke alarm numbers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_formulas_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: All five measures on one page, with the smoke alarm numbers

objects.text: Invented alarm numbers. Gold: the formulas, the page to keep.

slides.notes:
Before we leave the kitchen, here are the five measures together, because vendor reports print them like this. Each row is one question we built. Accuracy, how often is it right: ninety-six point two. Precision, when it rings is there a fire: thirty-two. Recall, the true positive rate, of the fires how many were caught: eighty.

False positive rate, of the quiet events how many rang: three and a half. And F1, precision and recall folded into one with the harmonic mean: forty-six. Every formula uses only the four counts from the confusion matrix. This page is on your take-away sheet. Now let me move from an invented alarm to a model trained on business data, where the same five questions apply.

title.text:
At work: a model scores each invoice
from 0 to 1 for the risk of late payment

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_hist_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: At work: a model scores each invoice from 0 to 1 for the risk of late payment

objects.text: Fictional Nile Valley Foods data. Positive: paid more than 30 days late. Test set: 900 invoices, 83 late.

runs.text: Score: a weighted sum of the features, turned into a number from 0 to 1.
Each bar: the share of its group in a band 0.05 wide.
Like smoke and toast, the groups overlap.

slides.notes:
Now the same ideas at work. An invoice is a bill sent to a shop, and some shops pay late. Our made-up Nile Valley Foods model reads each invoice's features, such as its amount, how long the shop has been a customer and how often it paid late last year, and gives a score from zero to one.

Inside, it is a weighted sum of those features, as in Session 1, turned into a number between zero and one; the method is called logistic regression. We judge it on nine hundred test invoices held back, as in Session 0, and never used for learning. Each bar shows what share of its group scored in a band zero point zero five wide.

Grey: the eight hundred and seventeen paid on time. Red: the eighty-three paid late.

title.text:
At threshold 0.20, the invoice model's confusion
matrix gives precision 34% and recall 42%

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_confusion_7.70x4.80_05527d63.png
objects.alt: At threshold 0.20, the invoice model's confusion matrix gives precision 34% and recall 42%

objects.text: Recorded run. Flag an invoice when its score is 0.20 or more.

slides.notes:
Pick a threshold, zero point two, and the scores become yes or no answers, just as smoke levels did. An invoice scoring zero point two or more is flagged as likely late. Out of nine hundred, the model flags a hundred and two. Thirty-five really were late: true positives.

Sixty-seven were paid on time: false positives. Forty-eight late invoices scored below the line: false negatives. Seven hundred and fifty were rightly left alone: true negatives. Same formulas as the alarm. Precision: thirty-five over thirty-five plus sixty-seven, thirty-four percent. Recall: thirty-five over thirty-five plus forty-eight, forty-two percent. F1: two times zero point three four times zero point four two, over zero point seven six, thirty-eight percent.

Which box would hurt your business most?

title.text:
The invoice model must beat two baselines:
the majority class and a simple rule

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_baselines_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The invoice model must beat two baselines: the majority class and a simple rule

objects.text: 817 of 900 were paid on time: always saying "on time" scores 90.8% accuracy.

runs.text: Majority class: recall 0%.
Rule, flag any shop late last year: precision 65 ÷ 445 = 15%, recall 65 ÷ 83 = 78%.
Model at 0.20: 34% and 42%.

slides.notes:
Whichever box hurts most, the model must first beat the baselines. The majority-class baseline says on time for every invoice. It is right eight hundred and seventeen times out of nine hundred, ninety point eight percent, and catches no late invoice. The second baseline is a plain rule a clerk could write: flag any shop that paid late at least once last year.

That rule flags four hundred and forty-five invoices and catches sixty-five of the eighty-three late ones: recall seventy-eight percent, but precision only sixty-five over four hundred and forty-five, fifteen percent. Our model at zero point two catches forty-two percent, with thirty-four percent of its flags right. Neither wins on both measures. If a vendor shows no baseline, ask for one.

title.text:
The same model at six thresholds: recall
climbs while precision and accuracy fall

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_thresholds_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The same model at six thresholds: recall climbs while precision and accuracy fall

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026: 900 test invoices, 83 late. Top row: majority-class baseline.

slides.notes:
The rule and the model differ mainly in where they draw the line, so here is what moving the line does. This is the result table from the recorded run, the same as the alarm table with more rows. Each row is the same model with a different threshold.

At zero point five the model flags only nine invoices, catches six, and misses seventy-seven. At zero point zero five it flags five hundred and twenty-six, and misses only five. Down the recall column: seven, eighteen, forty-two, fifty-two, sixty-five, ninety-four percent. Precision falls from sixty-seven to fifteen. Accuracy falls from ninety-one to fifty percent, worse than the majority-class baseline in the top row.

This is the second way a model looks good: one number that hides the threshold.

title.text:
The invoice model's ROC curve, one
dot per threshold, has an AUC of 0.80

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_roc_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The invoice model's ROC curve, one dot per threshold, has an AUC of 0.80

objects.text: Recorded run. Each red dot is one row of the table.

runs.text: AUC 0.80: a random late invoice outscores a random on-time one about 80 times in 100.

slides.notes:
The ROC curve draws that whole table as one picture, exactly as we built it for the alarm. Each red dot is one threshold. Up the side, the true positive rate: at zero point two, thirty-five of eighty-three late invoices, forty-two percent. Along the bottom, the false positive rate: sixty-seven of eight hundred and seventeen on-time invoices, eight percent.

The black line joins every possible threshold from the run. The gold area under it is the AUC, zero point eight. In words: pick one late and one on-time invoice at random, and about eighty times in a hundred the late one has the higher score. That says the model ranks invoices well.

It cannot tell you where to put the line, so what can?

title.text:
Choose the threshold with money:
the cost at 0.20, worked line by line

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_costcalc_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Choose the threshold with money: the cost at 0.20, worked line by line

objects.text: ASSUMED costs: UGX 20,000 to chase a flag, UGX 300,000 per missed late invoice.

slides.notes:
Money can choose the line, and this is where a finance manager feels at home. Suppose chasing a flagged invoice costs UGX 20,000 of staff time, and a missed late invoice costs UGX 300,000 in tied-up cash and follow-up. Those two figures are my assumption; you would use your own.

Staff chase every flag, right or wrong, so flags are true positives plus false positives: thirty-five plus sixty-seven, a hundred and two. A hundred and two times UGX 20,000 is UGX 2,040,000. The misses are the false negatives, forty-eight. Forty-eight times UGX 300,000 is UGX 14,400,000. Add the two: UGX 16,440,000.

In general, cost equals TP plus FP, times the chase cost, plus FN times the miss cost.

title.text:
The same sum at every threshold:
with these costs, 0.05 is the cheapest

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_cost_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The same sum at every threshold: with these costs, 0.05 is the cheapest

objects.text: Never flagging: 83 misses × UGX 300,000 = UGX 24.9 million.

runs.text: At 0.50: UGX 23.3 million.
At 0.20: UGX 16.4 million.
At 0.05: UGX 12.0 million.
If a miss costs UGX 100,000, then of 0.50, 0.20 and 0.05, 0.20 is cheapest.

slides.notes:
Do that same sum for every row and you get this chart. Never flagging anything means eighty-three misses at UGX 300,000 each: UGX 24.9 million. At zero point five the model flags nine and misses seventy-seven: UGX 23.3 million. At zero point two, the sum we just did, UGX 16.4 million.

At zero point zero five it flags five hundred and twenty-six and misses only five: UGX 12.0 million, the cheapest with these costs. Now change one assumption. If a miss costs only UGX 100,000, the recorded rerun shows that of the three thresholds zero point five, zero point two and zero point zero five, zero point two is cheapest.

The best line depends on what each mistake costs you, and the model cannot know that.

title.text: Which mistake costs more depends on the job

rows.text: A fine or a lost licence

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.34.png
objects.alt: coin

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.34.png
objects.alt: shield

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_phone_0.50.png
objects.alt: phone

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.34.png
objects.alt: people

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.34.png
objects.alt: gear

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.50.png
objects.alt: doc

objects.text: Equal costs are rare. Say which mistake hurts more before you choose a threshold.

slides.notes:
With my assumed costs the cheapest line was 0.05, but those two figures belong to one job. What each mistake costs changes with the job. In finance, a false negative, a missed late invoice, ties up cash, while a false positive costs a phone call. In compliance, a missed suspicious payment can cost a fine, and a false alarm costs an analyst an hour.

In customer service, a missed unhappy customer can be a lost shop. In HR, a missed strong candidate is a loss you never see. In operations, a missed breakdown costs a day of deliveries. In legal work, a privileged document handed over by mistake is serious, while a lawyer reading one extra costs minutes.

Which row is closest to your work?

title.text:
Demonstration 1: move the threshold,
change the costs, and read the row

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_9ba607ff.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 1: move the threshold, change the costs, and read the row

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Recall climbs, precision falls.
Accuracy gets worse while recall improves.
The cheapest row moves with the costs.

slides.notes:
You do not have to take the table or the costs on trust, so I will run them in front of you. I open a terminal and type the threshold script with three values, zero point five, zero point two and zero point zero five. It rebuilds the same made-up dataset and model every time, because the random seeds are fixed, so you should see the numbers from the table.

Watch three things. Recall climbs as the threshold falls. Precision falls. And accuracy gets worse while recall improves. Then I change the cost of a miss to UGX 100,000 and to UGX 600,000 and run again, and you watch the cheapest row move. If you want a value tried, tell me and I will type it.

title.text:
Overfitting: a model that memorises its
training cases does worse on new ones

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_overfit_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Overfitting: a model that memorises its training cases does worse on new ones

objects.text: Illustration. Red: late. Grey: on time. Red rings: two odd cases the model memorised.

runs.text: Training cases: memorising 20 of 20, line 18 of 20.
New cases: memorising 6 of 10, line 9 of 10.
A big gap between the two is the warning.

slides.notes:
The demonstration used only test invoices, and here is why that matters. Session 2 showed a tree that grew too deep; let me draw the idea. Each dot is a case, red late and grey on time. A simple model draws one straight line: red above, grey below.

It gets eighteen of twenty training cases right, missing two odd late cases among the grey. A memorising model adds a small ring around each odd case, so it scores twenty of twenty. Now new cases arrive. Grey cases that fall inside the rings are called late, and the memorising model gets six of ten, while the plain line gets nine.

Fitting the accidents of the training data, its noise, is overfitting. A big gap between the training score and the new-case score is the warning sign.

title.text:
Overfitting on the invoices: the deeper the tree,
the better on training and the worse on test

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_memorise_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Overfitting on the invoices: the deeper the tree, the better on training and the worse on test

objects.text: Depth: how many yes-or-no questions a tree may chain, as in Session 2. Recorded run.

runs.text: Depth 3: training 91.1%, test 90.1%.
Depth 21: training 100%, test 85.2%.
Majority-class baseline: 90.8%.

slides.notes:
Now the same thing on the real invoices. We trained decision trees, the kind you met last time, and allowed them more and more depth, meaning more yes or no questions chained one after another. The black line is the accuracy on the two thousand one hundred training invoices.

It climbs to a hundred percent. The red line is the accuracy on the nine hundred test invoices the trees never saw. It falls to eighty-five point two percent, below the majority-class baseline at ninety point eight. A tree three questions deep scores ninety-one point one on training and ninety point one on test: a small gap.

Like the rings in the picture, the deep tree has memorised its training set, accidents included. This is the third way a model looks good without being good.

title.text:
Demonstration 2: a deep tree
overfits, and the baseline shows it

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_versus_7.30x3.90_efe84b90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 2: a deep tree overfits, and the baseline shows it

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Training accuracy 100%, test accuracy 85.2%.
The majority-class baseline scores 90.8%.
A small tree, depth 3: 91.1% training, 90.1% test.

slides.notes:
Let me show you that overfitting in the real output. I run the measuring script from the demo folder. It prints the baselines, the threshold table and the trees. Look for the deep tree: twenty-one questions deep, with two hundred and twenty-nine leaves, the final answers at the ends of its paths, and a hundred percent on the training invoices.

Then look at the test score, eighty-five point two. Next to it, the majority-class baseline scores ninety point eight. A small tree, three questions deep, scores ninety-one percent on training invoices and ninety on test invoices, which is honest but no better than doing nothing. The lesson: ask for the score on the test set, and for the baseline beside it.

title.text:
Twenty real cases from the test set: the
model flags a case at a score of 0.20 or more

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_cases_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Twenty real cases from the test set: the model flags a case at a score of 0.20 or more

objects.text: Drawn from the recorded run. Gold shows the invoices that really were paid late.

slides.notes:
You have the ideas, so now it is your turn with a pencil. This is your exercise sheet. It lists twenty invoices drawn from the real test set of the recorded run. For each one you see the invoice number, the amount, the score the model gave it, and whether it really was paid late, shown in gold.

Six of the twenty were late. The rule for the model is simple: a score of zero point two or more means positive, flagged. Read down the list once before you start, and notice that some late invoices score very low. Those will be false negatives. Then you fill in the confusion matrix and work out precision and recall.

title.text:
Fill the confusion matrix from the twenty
cases, then work out precision and recall

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Count the twenty cases into the four cells.

runs.text: Flag every case with a score of 0.20 or more.
Count TP, FP, FN and TN. They add to 20.
Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP).
Recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN).

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_blank_5.50x3.55.png
objects.alt: A blank two by two confusion matrix with the precision and recall formulas

objects.text: You keep: The filled matrix and two percentages. The worksheet.

slides.notes:
Here is what you do with those twenty cases. Take fifteen minutes. Work alone or in pairs, with a pencil and the worksheet. First, go down the list and mark every case with a score of zero point two or more as flagged. Second, count the four cells: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

They must add up to twenty, which is your check. Third, work out precision as true positives divided by true positives plus false positives. Fourth, work out recall as true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives. Write each as a fraction first, then as a percentage.

I will walk round. When you have finished, compare with your neighbour and ask why any answers differ.

title.text:
Move the threshold by hand: raise
it to 0.50, then lower it to 0.15

objects.text: 5 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Redo the counts at two new thresholds.

runs.text: Cross out your flags and flag again at 0.50.
Fill the first row of the small table.
Do the same at 0.15.
Say which threshold you would choose, and why.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_3f07784e.png
objects.alt: A small table to fill in at three thresholds, with the 0.20 row already done

objects.text: You keep: Two rows of the table and one sentence.

slides.notes:
Keep your answers, because the same twenty cases give you a second exercise of five minutes. Change the threshold in your head. First raise it to zero point five and recount. Fill in the first row of the small table. Then lower it to zero point fifteen and fill in the third row.

The middle row, zero point two, is already done from your last exercise, so you can check yourself against it. I walk round again. Look at what happens to precision and recall as the threshold moves. Then write one sentence saying which threshold you would choose for a late-payment model, and what it would cost you in false positives or false negatives.

title.text:
Six questions to put to any
vendor about the numbers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.69.png
objects.alt: folder

objects.text: What test data was it measured on? Had it seen it?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.69.png
objects.alt: flag

objects.text: How common is the case? What does the majority class score?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_switch_0.69.png
objects.alt: switch

objects.text: What are precision and recall, at which threshold?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.69.png
objects.alt: coin

objects.text: Who chose the threshold? What did each mistake cost?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.69.png
objects.alt: people

objects.text: How does it compare with a simple rule or today?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.69.png
objects.alt: check

objects.text: Can we test it on 50 of our own cases?

slides.notes:
You have now done by hand what a vendor's single number hides, so here is what to ask. When a vendor says, our model is ninety-five percent accurate, you now have six questions. What test data was that measured on, and had the model seen it?

How common is the thing you are looking for, and what would the majority-class baseline score?

What are precision and recall, and at which threshold?

Who chose the threshold, and what did each kind of mistake cost?

How does it compare with a simple rule or with how we do it today?

And can we test it on fifty of our own cases before we sign?

The full one-page sheet has four more, about monitoring, drift and who checks.

title.text:
Which mistake would cost your business
more: a false positive or a false negative?

objects.text: Think of the task you would most like a model to help with. Which mistake costs more?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.80.png
objects.alt: shield

objects.text: A false negative
Set the threshold low. Accept more false positives. Ask for recall.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.80.png
objects.alt: check

objects.text: A false positive
Set the threshold high. Ask for precision.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_chart_0.80.png
objects.alt: chart

objects.text: About equal
Balance them. Ask for F1 and the threshold used.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.80.png
objects.alt: coin

objects.text: I do not know yet
Put a UGX figure on each mistake first.
Write the task, the costlier mistake and a first UGX figure for each in your workbook.

slides.notes:
In the exercise you saw that the best threshold moves with the cost of each mistake, so bring that back to your own work. Think of one task you would like a model to help with: an alert, a shortlist, a sort. Ask yourself which mistake costs more, a false positive or a false negative.

If a false negative costs more, you want the threshold low and you should ask the vendor for recall. If a false positive costs more, set it high and ask for precision. If they are about equal, ask for F1 and the threshold. And if you do not know, that is the finding: put a UGX figure on each mistake before you buy anything. Say your answer aloud to the group.

Keep the vendor question sheet, and
put it to the next proposal you read

Keep the vendor question sheet. It is one page of ten questions about the numbers behind an AI claim, with the five measures we built today. Put it next to the next proposal you read, and ask the questions before you ask about price. Every example today was a table of numbers.

Session 4 starts a new topic: how a computer turns words into numbers, and then measures how close two of them are, with the distance idea from Session 2. You need to prepare nothing for it.

We began with this question: How do I know whether a model is any good, and what should I ask the vendor who says it is? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
